title: Convert Sorted Array to Binary Search Tree
description:
Given an integer array `nums` whose elements are sorted in **strictly ascending order**, convert it into a **height-balanced** binary search tree (BST).

A binary tree is **height-balanced** if, for every node in the tree, the depths of its left and right subtrees differ by at most `1`. A binary search tree satisfies that for every node, all values in its left subtree are strictly less than the node's value and all values in its right subtree are strictly greater than the node's value.

If multiple height-balanced BSTs are possible, you may return **any** valid one. The judge validates that your returned tree is a valid BST containing the exact elements of `nums` and is height-balanced (`true`).
constraints: nums is sorted in a strictly increasing order.
hints: To keep the tree height-balanced, both subtrees of every node should contain nearly the same number of elements.
Choosing the middle element of the current subarray as the root splits the remaining elements evenly into the left half (all smaller) and the right half (all larger).
Recursively build the left and right subtrees using index bounds [lo, hi] rather than slicing arrays so the total work stays O(n).

examples.explanation: Choosing 0 as root yields [-10, -3] on the left and [5, 9] on the right; both [0,-3,9,-10,null,5] and [0,-10,5,null,-3,null,9] are valid height-balanced BSTs.
Both [1,null,3] and [3,1] are valid height-balanced BSTs for [1, 3].
A single-element array forms a single-node BST [0], which is trivially height-balanced.
